title: Function limits, one-sided limits, and epsilon–delta reasoning
section: Limits of Functions ▷ Definitions and calculations
terms: limit of a function; epsilon–delta definition; punctured neighborhood; sequential criterion; left-hand limit; right-hand limit.

exposition.text:
The statement lim f(x) = L means that for each ε > 0 some δ > 0 makes 0 < |x − a| < δ
x→a
imply |f(x) − L| < ε for domain points. The value at a is excluded and may be undefined.
Equivalently, every sequence of domain points x ̸= a with x → a must satisfy f(x ) → L.
n n n
Testing only one sequence is insufficient.
Left and right limits restrict to x < a and x > a. At a two-sided accumulation point, the
two-sided finite limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and agree. Algebraic limit
laws and squeezing apply. For floor functions and absolute values, determine their formula on
each side before substituting; cancellation is legitimate on a punctured neighborhood even if the
original expression is undefined at the limit point.

question.text:

For x ̸= 0, let f(x) = 1 + |x| − 1 /x. What are its left and right limits at zero, respectively?
(A) (1/2, 1/2)
(B) (−1/2, 1/2)
(C) (−1, 1)
(D) (0, 0)
(E) Neither one-sided limit exists.

solution.text:
q
Rationalizing gives f(x) = |x|/[x( 1 + |x| + 1)]. The factor |x|/x is −1 on the left and 1 on
the right, yielding the stated pair.

question.text:
Let f(x) = ⌊x⌋ + ⌊−x⌋. Which statement holds at every integer m?
(A) lim f(x) = f(m) = 0.
x→m
(B) The left limit is −1 and the right limit is 0.
(C) The two-sided limit fails to exist.
(D) lim f(x) = −1, whereas f(m) = 0.
x→m
(E) lim f(x) = 1.
x→m

solution.text:
For noninteger x, ⌊−x⌋ = −⌊x⌋ − 1, so f(x) = −1. At integer m the sum is 0. A sufficiently
small punctured neighborhood contains no other integer, so both one-sided limits equal −1.

What is lim (x − 8)/(x − 4)?
x→2
(A) 6
(B) The limit does not exist
(C) 3
(D) 2
(E) 4

solution.text:
2
Cancel x − 2 to obtain (x + 2x + 4)/(x + 2) for x ̸= 2. Evaluation at 2 gives 12/4 = 3.

(A) I only (B) II only (C) I and III only (D) II and III only (E) I, II, and III

solution.text:
I is the sequential criterion. If the limit fails, some ε > 0 admits bad points arbitrarily close
to a. Infinitely many lie on one side; choose them successively closer on that side to form a
monotone bad sequence, disproving III. II is insufficient: sin(π/(x − a)) vanishes on a ± 1/n
but has no limit.
